title: The walk is a trail of sealed addresses
caption: The envelope is one row lookup; its contents are the byte and the next row address. The wait lies before that next address is known. The analogy breaks at the postman: cache hits can be quick and other work can overlap a miss; neither every load nor every decoder thread must stall.
mapping: Envelope = row lookup; enclosed address = dependency; hourglass = a possible exposed cache-miss delay.
placement: Opening, after the paragraph labelled “The walk”, ending “and building it adds more.”
explains: Puts the unavailable next request on the far side of the wait, rather than merely drawing an LF arrow.
evidence: Journal §1 (LF/its inverse and emission); §6 (dependent walk and cache counts). Conceptual dependence, no new measured latency.

title: One instruction moves the whole tray
caption: Each compartment is a row in one equal-byte run; the tray is that run’s interval, and sliding it is LF’s constant offset. The unchanged spacing explains why one interval describes all four mappings. The analogy breaks at physical movement: this describes a map; the kernel does not move the stored bytes in a tray, and the shift can also be negative.
mapping: Tray = maximal equal-byte run; compartment = row; displacement = LF offset.
placement: Opening, after the paragraph labelled “One shift per run”, ending “a run averages about 14 rows.”
explains: Shows the invariant that makes compression possible: all relative offsets survive one common translation.
evidence: Journal §1: LF(x)=C(L[x])+occurrences before x, hence constant LF(x)−x within a run. Toy addresses chosen only to show translation.

title: A ticket can remember a longer journey
caption: The number of tickets is an interval’s remaining row count; the stamp is its return word, in reconstruction order. Shortening the longer interval leaves the shorter one representing a longer journey. The lower stack is a separate, generic batch: all occurrences of the chosen pair occupy one cell and share one rule. Counted steps per byte: Wikidata 0.1309, prose 0.6761, uniform random bytes about 1; short runs leave less to batch. The analogy breaks at the stamp: the implementation records that rule once, not once per ticket; expanding it still has to emit the bytes.
mapping: Ticket count = interval length; stamp = word, not length; cut = removed endpoint rows; stack = occurrences represented by one cell.
placement: §1, replace the existing “Two steps rebuild aab” interval-strip figure, immediately after the paragraph defining B,A and A,B. Keep the subsequent worked-example paragraphs.
explains: Makes the otherwise surprising distinction visible: one remaining row can represent two emitted bytes. The generic batch adds the reason a step amortises over rows.
evidence: Journal §2 top-wins rule and equal case; §5.6 Theorem 2 digram-cell equivalence. aab gives A:2,a and B:1,b → A:1,a and B:1,ab. Generic stack is not a second aab census.

title: Keep finished work still
caption: Hanging cards are letters in the two linked orders; their strings are links that must be patched. A filed receipt is a completed cell, while the clipboard is the live remainder and promised next slot. Keeping completed work still removes the relinking work, and known future addresses permit prefetch. The analogy breaks at the filing cabinet: two slots are written for a cell, destinations can be scattered, and word/output processing still writes memory; this is not a claim that the decoder writes each byte only once.
mapping: Card = linked-order letter; string = neighbour link; filed receipt = completed cell; clipboard = live register/pending-slot state.
placement: §3 “Why the cells kernel is cheaper”, insert after paragraph 2 beginning “A cell is the overlap”. This section has no figure in the rewritten post.
explains: Makes the removed operation concrete—rewiring old state—and separates immutable finished cells from mutable unfinished work.
evidence: Journal §3.1 (5–6 links), §3.5 (two slots, promised slots, remainder in registers, prefetch); §6.2 staged ten-block, one-run-per-stage timings. Does not attribute the full gain to write-once cells alone.

title: The planner is on the clock too
caption: A stop is a cell step; the route is their order, and the magnifying glasses are the search for the next eligible step. The second order takes steps that create no new boundary first, otherwise the largest cell. These “free” steps still cost CPU work. The analogy breaks at distance: routes and drawn stops are schematic, not a scale of counts, memory distance or time; 1.220 is a lower bound for this cell-step model, not every inversion algorithm. A different worklist variant was priced higher from counts and estimated costs; it was not a timed comparison of these two orders.
mapping: Stop = step; route = schedule; magnifier = candidate/segment search. Numeric labels alone encode the measured counts; no length or stop-count scale.
placement: §5 “Fewer steps by a different order”, replace the existing step-count bar figure after the three counts are introduced.
explains: Adds a visible competing expense to the tempting shorter schedule, without turning a step count into a stopwatch result.
evidence: Journal §5.6 exact identity S=r₂−1+U and counts 1.812/1.279/1.220; §8 different worklist (free-first, else right end): 1.458 steps/run on ten blocks, 2.25 segment ends tested/step, two steps in three at another segment; 150 versus 115 instructions/run is a cost model with two estimated unit costs, not timing.

title: The rules are a book’s nested bindings
caption: Each bound part is a word; its binding seam is the standard Lyndon split, before its smallest proper suffix. Reading the joins from the smaller book upward gives the rules ab = a·b and aab = a·ab. The analogy breaks at the bookbinder: the kernel does not first sort suffixes or build a separate book tree, and shared equal rules form a grammar rather than a physically duplicated tree. The stated identity concerns right-end induction’s expanded tree for a primitive block’s least rotation.
mapping: Book = word; nested binding = binary concatenation; seam = smallest-proper-suffix split; opening = expansion.
placement: §4 “The Lyndon tree”, replace “How the row map leads to the Lyndon tree”, after paragraph 3 ending with the Crochemore–Russo reference.
explains: Turns a static tree into reversible assembly: the same joins that built the word determine its nested parts. The caption names the split rule so this is not just an arbitrary parse tree.
evidence: Journal §5.6 Theorem 1 and §10: Hohlweg–Reutenauer identity and Tsuruta et al. shared Lyndon SLP. Primitive/least-rotation qualification retained.
